extracted.intended_audience: students and experimenters in hydrostatics/physics (readers of classical experimental hydrostatics)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, experimental methods, and quantitative rules for comparing lateral (side) and perpendicular (downward) pressure of fluids, and for analysing devices such as syphons and fountains. Includes experimental set-ups, calculational rules, and practical simplifications (e.g., neglecting air weight in many cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral Preſſure accommodates to the perpendicular Height of the Water
rubrics_metrics.description: “the lateral Preſſure accommodates itſelf to the perpendicular Height of the Water, and fo is greater or leſs accordingly; and each Point ... has a different Height of Water above it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: lateral (side) pressure at a given point on a vertical surface depends on the vertical column of fluid above that point (the perpendicular height), so different points on the same vertical plane experience different lateral pressures. To compare lateral pressures you must compare heights over corresponding small parts. Example in text: points A, B, C, D, E each have different heights a b, c d, e f, g h, i, hence different lateral pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide surfaces into very small Parts (points) to avoid calculation error
rubrics_metrics.description: “the ſmaller the Parts or Points are into which AE and EI are divi­ded, the leſſer is the difference of the Heights and Depths of Water ... and conſequently theſe Diverſities ... will produce the ſmaller Change in the Calculations”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for analysis: model vertical or horizontal faces as being composed of many very small elements (points). As element size → 0, variation of heights across an element becomes negligible and sums/integrals converge; this reduces error in comparing lateral vs perpendicular pressures. Practical experimental advice: take parts very small (mere points) to make theoretical sums match experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of lateral and perpendicular preſſure for equal Heights (experimental observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: (experimental claim) that “the lateral Preſſure which ſuch a little Part ... undergoes in the Perpendicular AE, equal, or at leaſt does not ſenſibly differ from the Preſſure downward, which a Horizontal equal Part ... has an equal Height of Water over it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental method: use a bottle with small holes and a glass tube (Musschenbroek instrument) so that the small parts compared have essentially the same heights; observe that water scarcely flows when tube/hole removed, and heights in tube and vessel remain the same. Conclusion valid when parts are taken sufficiently small so heights differ negligibly. The text gives a detailed bottle/tube set-up and step-by-step observations supporting this equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Hydrostatical Law of Lateral Preſſure (relation to horizontal pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the lateral Preſſure upon A E being, in this Caſe, 10 fb. is the half of 20 tb. or of the Preſſure downwards, which the ſaid A E if it lay horizontallly at E I, level with the loweſt Point E, wou'd ſuffer from its incumbent Water A E Ig.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule for comparing pressures: to find lateral pressure on a vertical plane AE when fluid stands to height AK, set AE horizontally (as EI) at the level of the lowest point E; the downward pressure on that horizontal plane from the same overlying water AE Ig equals twice the lateral pressure on AE. In other words (as applied here) lateral pressure on a vertical rectangular element equals half the downward pressure that the corresponding horizontal element would sustain under the same fluid distribution. The text demonstrates this by decomposing surfaces into equal parts and summing weights (example numbers given: lateral 10 lb vs downward 20 lb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental procedure to compare lateral and perpendicular preſſures (bottle/tube set‑up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed experiment: drill small holes in the side and bottom of a bottle, insert a glass tube sealed with cork and soldered joints, fill to certain heights, stop/unstop holes and observe heights in the vessel and tube; inference: columns of air/water balance and lateral vs perpendicular pressures can be compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise guidance included: make holes (ab, P), plug P, insert a sealed small transverse tube across ab with horizontal orifice fg, fill vessel to height RT, fill tube EW, remove finger from fg and observe water spouting and settling; then remove small tube and observe no appreciable change in water heights — concluding equality of pressures for sufficiently small parts. Use of Musschenbroek's small glass instrument recommended. Also describes repeated trials (since 1696) and notes to account for air contraction/expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral preſſure adapts to Height, not to Breadth (breadth invariance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Powers of the lateral Preſſure remain the ſame whether the Breadth of the Water be increas'd or diminiſh'd; but that upon augmenting or leſſening the Height of Water, thoſe Powers are accordingly augmented or leſſen'd.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental demonstration: place a partition that halves the breadth of water pressing on a board while keeping the water at the same height — lateral pressure on the board remains the same. Practical implication: when predicting lateral force on a plane, vary height factors, not breadth, for pressure per unit area; total force still depends on area but pressure distribution depends on depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the surrounding Air on lateral Preſſure is negligibly small
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculation and statement: though a column of air above the water exerts lateral pressure, its effect on the water's lateral pressure is very small (water ≈ 1000× heavier than air), so surrounding air lessens lateral pressure only by an imperceptible fraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative guidance: in the numerical example the surrounding air lessens lateral pressure by 1/1000th (expressed in text as a 5; part in context), making no sensible alteration in the experiments described. Therefore for most practical hydrostatic calculations the weight of air may be neglected; the text nevertheless shows how to include it in precise balance-of-columns calculations when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place measuring (balance) arm at the Center of Pressure for accurate measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental note: “the preſſing Part ... of the Ballance AE F, muſt be placed exactly upon the Point of the Wood A, where the Center is, or where the lateral Preſſure is ſtrongeſt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring lateral pressure with a lever/balance against a wooden plank or board, align the lever's contacting point with the true center of pressure; raising or lowering the lever relative to that center changes the measured resisting weight substantially and leads to erroneous results. The text reports experimental variation when the axis was higher or lower than the true center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral Preſſure on a compound plane equals the sum of contributions from its small Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure shown: divide vertical plane AE into equal (or many small) parts A,B,C,D,E and sum the lateral pressure contributions of each part according to the column of water over it (weights 1,2,3,4,... in text example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing total lateral force on a vertical plane that is non-uniformly submerged, decompose the plane into many small horizontal strips/points, compute lateral pressure contribution for each from its local depth, then sum (integrate) to obtain the total lateral force. The text uses small integer-weight examples (1,2,3,4) to show the total lateral vs downward pressures and that the lateral sums amount to half the corresponding downward sum in the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syphon operation derived from difference of column weights (air+water)
rubrics_metrics.description: “this ſhows the Force wherewith a Syphon flows, ... the Water at the Orifice of the Tube I K, is by the lately mention'd difference of Weight 'between the two Columns ... preſs'd or protruded downwards ... equal to the Weight by which the Water Column RQK ... exceeds the Air‑Column R S T V.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical rule: stop the syphon so fluid is quiescent, identify corresponding horizontal planes, express pressures as weights of the air and water columns on each side (e.g., a, b, c in the text). On removing the stopper, the net driving force (and hence flow) equals the difference between the total downward‑pressing columns and the upward‑pressing columns — effectively the excess weight of the water column over the counteracting air (and water) column. The text gives a numerical illustration (e.g., 100+10 minus 100+1 gives net 9 lb in that toy example) showing how to translate into net flow force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fountain jet force = weight of certain water columns minus weight of certain air columns (design rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Water ... will be protruded out of the Cock M O with a Force equal to the Weight of both the Water‑Columns 2 R and Y Z, Subtracting the Gravity of the two Air‑Columns T 3 and 4 M.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design/analysis rule for multi‑cistern/closed‑air fountains: compute the upward force at the nozzle as (sum of weights of the contributing water columns) − (sum of weights of the opposing air columns). The example in the text yields a numerical difference (e.g., 1170 less 1008 = 162 lb) and notes that because air is much lighter than water the air terms may be neglected for practical estimation, hence the jet behaves approximately as if driven by the height of the relevant water columns alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion of Fluids results from removing a Resistance; pressure differences determine direction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Motion may likewise be produced by removing a Resistance which obstructed Motion ... all will stand still, and your Finger will become the Impediment or Reſiſtance of Motion. ... So that this Resistance ... being taken away, a Motion will be made towards the Side of the Resistance; and even with that Force with which the Resistance was preſs'd when the Fluids were quieſcent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental/interpretive rule: a fluid at rest may be in balance because of an external obstruction (finger, plug). Removing that obstruction allows the existing imbalance of pressures to produce motion toward the previously resisted side, with a force corresponding to the earlier pressure difference. Use this to reason about valve, syphon, and nozzle behaviour; the text gives the blow‑into‑tube/finger example to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experimental verification of hydrostatical deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial methodological stance: though mathematical demonstrations exist (e.g., Kevin), the text states a preference to deduce proofs from experiments and adds specific experiments to render conclusions more certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When establishing hydrostatic laws apply both deductive calculation and direct experiment. The text supplies multiple experimental arrangements (quadrilateral vessel with removable plug, balance measurements, bottle/tube experiments, fountains and syphons) and omits the full algebraic calculations 'for brevity sake' but shows how experiments confirm the calculational rules; practical advice: perform apparatus trials to confirm theoretical expectations before generalizing.
